summary.text: The graph of a function f is the set of ordered pairs (x, y) where f(x) = y.
When x and f(x) are real numbers, these pairs are Cartesian coordinates of points in a plane and often form a curve.
For a function of two variables the graph is a set of ordered triples, which for a continuous real-valued function forms a surface in three-dimensional space.

facts.label: Two variables
facts.value: The graph is a set of triples, forming a surface

facts.label: Set theory view
facts.value: A function is actually equal to its graph

facts.label: Missing information
facts.value: A graph alone does not determine the codomain

items.prompt: A function's graph includes the point where x is 2 and y is 5. What does that say about the function?

options.label: Its output for the input 2 is 5
Its output for the input 5 is 2
Its outputs always add up to 7
Its input values stop at 5

items.explain: The graph is the set of pairs (x, y) where f(x) = y, so this point means f(2) = 5.

items.prompt: A function takes two inputs and gives one output. What is its graph made of?

options.label: Pairs of numbers on a flat plane, as before
Sets of triples that form a surface in three-dimensional space
A single number for each pair of inputs
A pair of curves drawn on the same axes

items.explain: For functions of two variables the graph is the set of ordered triples (x, y, z) where f(x, y) = z, a subset of three-dimensional space.

items.prompt: Looking only at a function's graph, can you tell which whole set its outputs are allowed to come from?

options.label: Yes, it is the highest and lowest points shown
Yes, provided the graph is continuous
Yes, it is the same as the set of inputs
No, the graph on its own does not determine it

items.explain: A function as a mapping also has a domain and a codomain, and the graph of a function on its own does not determine the codomain.

items.prompt: A mathematician says that in set theory a function and its graph are the same object. Why do people still use both words?

options.label: They are different objects after all
Each term views the same object from a different perspective
One covers only curves, the other only surfaces
The graph word is kept for pictures with colours

items.explain: Even if considered the same object, the two terms indicate viewing it from a different perspective.

items.prompt: A function gives the output 7 at the input 3. Is the point with x equal to 3 and y equal to 10 on its graph?

options.label: Yes, any point with x equal to 3 is on it
Yes, if the curve passes near it
No, only pairs (x, f(x)) belong, and here y is 7
No, since 10 is bigger than the input

items.explain: The graph contains exactly the pairs (x, y) where f(x) = y, and f(3) = 7.

items.prompt: Formally, a function is made up of which three parts?

options.label: Its inputs, its outputs and its slope
Its domain, its codomain and its graph
Its curve, its surface and its plot
Its variables, its constants and its sum

items.explain: Formally, a function is formed by the triple consisting of its domain, its codomain and its graph.
